The evidence, as of the release: the workspace tests (wiremock for the client, no network in the default run); the ten ignored live tests in `crates/judgment/tests/live.rs`, all passing against `laya-serve` ([judgment against Laya typed-decisions](../verification/laya-typed-decisions.md)); the committed Laya recordings, which still replay to an accuracy of 0.725 on 200 questions under the stricter decoder; and signalman's committed Jev recordings (`examples/eval/runs/jev-1.13.0`), which replay to a decision agreement of 1.00. None of the 0.2 behaviour had been checked against a live TypeSafe account at the release: the hosted API had answered this client once, under 0.1. It has since: the ten live tests passed against the hosted API on 2026-10-03 ([judgment against the hosted TypeSafe API](../verification/hosted-typesafe.md)). The full list of changes, the breaking ones included, is in the crate's [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/chussenot/signalman/blob/main/crates/judgment/CHANGELOG.md).

# Decisions

A record captures one architecturally significant decision: the problem, the options weighed, the choice and what it costs, in [MADR](https://adr.github.io/madr/) form. The records here govern the crate's own design.

Record numbers are shared with [signalman's records](https://github.com/chussenot/signalman/blob/main/docs/decisions/README.md): there is one sequence for the repository, and a record lives with the code it governs. A number is an identifier, never reused or renumbered, so `decision 0003` means the same record wherever it is cited.

| Id | Title | Status |
|---|---|---|
| [0003](0003-typed-handles-between-questions-and-answers.md) | Typed handles between questions and answers | accepted |

Signalman's records that shaped the crate, read with these:

- [0002 Calibrated judgments over generated text](https://github.com/chussenot/signalman/blob/main/docs/decisions/0002-calibrated-judgments-over-generated-text.md): why System One primitives at all.
- [0010 Extract the judgment core into a reusable crate](https://github.com/chussenot/signalman/blob/main/docs/decisions/0010-extract-the-judgment-core-into-a-crate.md): what became the crate, what stayed in the application, and why the existing crates were not adopted.
- [0011 Documentation lives with its concern](https://github.com/chussenot/signalman/blob/main/docs/decisions/0011-documentation-lives-with-its-concern.md): why these pages are here and not under signalman's `docs/`.

## Status notes

Records are not edited after acceptance; a fact that has moved since is noted here.

- 0003 was written in signalman's `docs/decisions/` before the crate existed, and moved here with its number on 2026-10-03 (decision 0011). Its "More information" link was the one line changed: the page it pointed to was split, and the link now names both halves.

To add a record, follow [signalman's procedure](https://github.com/chussenot/signalman/blob/main/docs/decisions/README.md#writing-a-record) with the next number of the shared sequence, and put the record here when it governs the crate.


<!-- source: crates/judgment/docs/decisions/0003-typed-handles-between-questions-and-answers.md -->


# 0003 Typed handles between questions and answers

## Context and problem statement

The TypeSafe API takes a map of question ids to questions and returns a map of the same ids to answers. Nothing on the wire connects a Noul question to a Noul answer, and a Choice answer's option is a string. How should the Rust client expose answers so that consumers cannot misread them?

## Decision drivers

- A misread number in a paging decision is worse than a failed request
- Request criteria and answer parsing must not drift apart
- Runtime option sets (incident references, catalog groups) must remain possible
- The client should stay small enough to read in one sitting

## Considered options

1. Typed handles: adding a question returns `Handle<A>`; `Response::get(&handle)` performs a checked conversion; closed option sets are enums generated by a macro
2. Raw maps: return the parsed JSON and let each consumer check the primitive and parse strings
3. A fully typed request struct per use case, with serde deriving both the request and the response shape

## Decision outcome

Chosen option: "Typed handles". `Questions::noul`, `choice`, `score` and `dynamic_choice` return `Handle<A>`. `Response::get` checks the primitive and converts. Closed option sets are enums implementing `Options`, generated by the `options!` macro, which also produces the request criteria.

### Consequences

- Good, because the request and the parser derive from one definition and cannot disagree
- Good, because a primitive mismatch or unknown option is an explicit error naming the question
- Good, because runtime option sets use `dynamic_choice`, and the boundary is visible in the type (`Choice<String>`)
- Bad, because there is more ceremony than a raw JSON call; the saving is paid back by every consumer

### Confirmation

`src/answer.rs` tests cover mismatch, unknown option, missing answer and out-of-range probabilities. `Probability` and `Confidence` are distinct validated newtypes.

## Pros and cons of the options

### Typed handles

- Good, because errors surface at the one place strings become types
- Good, because handles are cheap markers; nothing extra crosses the wire
- Bad, because `dynamic_choice` consumers still map string keys back to their own data

### Raw maps

- Good, because it is the smallest possible client
- Bad, because every consumer re-checks primitives and re-parses strings, and a typo is found at runtime if at all

### Typed request struct per use case

- Good, because serde does the work
- Bad, because the API's map shape does not fit a struct per use case without a custom (de)serializer per struct, and speculative questions make the shape vary per request

## More information

[How judgment works](../design.md#typed-handles); how signalman reads its triage answers through the handles: [TypeSafe client](https://github.com/chussenot/signalman/blob/main/docs/typesafe-client.md).
